items.prompt: An internal service name should resolve only inside two application VPCs. Which Route 53 design is appropriate?
constraints: The service has no public DNS requirement.
The two VPCs are in supported Regions and accounts.
Other VPCs must not resolve the name by default.

options.text: Create a private hosted zone and associate it explicitly with the two application VPCs, then create the required records.
Create a public hosted zone because every Route 53 record is visible to the internet.
Add the service name to an IAM policy because IAM controls private DNS visibility.
Attach the private zone to the organization root so every VPC receives the records automatically.

feedback.Reason: Private hosted zones answer queries from associated VPCs, so explicit association is the access boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A private hosted zone is associated with selected VPCs and is resolved through the VPC DNS path. Association does not automatically extend to every VPC in an organization.
Details.scenarioApplication: The DNS owner associates only the application VPCs, validates resolver behavior from each subnet, and records the zone owner and association list.
Details.errorCorrection: Public zones publish publicly, IAM does not control DNS association, and organization hierarchy is not a private hosted-zone association by itself.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Explicit associations limit visibility but require lifecycle automation when application VPCs are added or removed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A public hosted zone would expose the name through public DNS rather than keep it VPC-private.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM policies authorize API actions and do not make a hosted zone resolve in a VPC.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Private-zone associations are explicit VPC relationships, not automatic OU or organization-root inheritance.

items.prompt: The same application name must resolve to an internal load balancer for VPC clients and a public endpoint for internet clients. Which approach fits?
constraints: Internal and external clients use the same fully qualified name.
The internal address must not be published publicly.
The public service remains internet reachable.

options.text: Use a private hosted zone associated with the VPC for the internal answer and a separate public hosted zone for the public answer, with deliberate DNS ownership.
Put both private and public addresses in one public zone and rely on clients to choose the private record.
Use an internet gateway route to make public DNS answers private for VPC clients.
Create two IAM roles with the same name because DNS view selection is identity-based.

feedback.Reason: Split-horizon DNS uses private and public authoritative views so the same name has context-specific answers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 private hosted zones answer associated VPC queries, while public hosted zones answer public DNS queries. The private zone can override the public view for clients inside the VPC.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team creates an internal alias to the internal load balancer, publishes only the public target publicly, and tests both resolver contexts.
Details.errorCorrection: A public zone does not keep a private address private, routes do not rewrite DNS answers, and IAM roles do not select hosted-zone views.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Split-horizon naming preserves a stable application name but increases record ownership and troubleshooting complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Publishing private addresses in a public zone violates the privacy boundary and does not provide context-aware answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network routing does not transform a public DNS response into a private one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS view selection is not based on IAM role names.

items.prompt: On-premises clients must resolve records in a Route 53 private hosted zone. Which component provides the VPC-side DNS entry point?
constraints: The hybrid network route already reaches the VPC.
The clients use their on-premises DNS servers.
The private names should not be published publicly.

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC and configure the on-premises DNS servers to forward the private namespace to its addresses.
Create a public hosted zone because on-premises clients cannot query private zones through a network path.
Create a NAT gateway and use its public address as the private DNS resolver.
Use a VPC gateway endpoint because endpoint routes resolve private hosted-zone records.

feedback.Reason: A Resolver inbound endpoint accepts DNS queries from external networks and resolves names using the VPC Resolver context.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inbound endpoint IP addresses are placed in selected subnets and receive forwarded queries from on-premises DNS servers. Security groups and hybrid routing must permit DNS traffic.
Details.scenarioApplication: The DNS team creates redundant endpoint IPs, adds conditional forwarding on premises, and tests both the query path and private-zone association.
Details.errorCorrection: Public publication is unnecessary, NAT is not a DNS Resolver endpoint, and gateway endpoints do not answer private hosted-zone queries.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Inbound endpoints extend private naming to on-premises but add endpoint cost, security-group rules, and DNS dependency management.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private names can be resolved over a hybrid path through Resolver inbound endpoints without public publication.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A NAT gateway translates egress traffic and is not a DNS query endpoint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Gateway endpoints provide service traffic paths, not Route 53 Resolver forwarding.

items.prompt: VPC workloads must resolve an internal hostname owned by the corporate DNS servers. Which AWS-side configuration is required?
constraints: The VPC can route to the corporate DNS servers.
Only a specific corporate namespace should leave the VPC.
Other DNS queries should continue to use the VPC Resolver.

options.text: Create a Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule for the corporate namespace, then associate the rule with the workload VPC.
Create an inbound endpoint because outbound endpoints are only for public DNS lookups.
Add a private hosted-zone record for every corporate hostname and remove the corporate DNS dependency.
Use a NAT gateway as the conditional forwarding rule target.

feedback.Reason: Resolver outbound endpoints and forwarding rules send selected VPC queries to DNS servers outside the VPC.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A forwarding rule matches a domain suffix and sends queries through an outbound endpoint to target IP addresses. Rule association determines which VPCs use it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The DNS owner forwards only the corporate suffix, retains the default AWS resolver for other names, and validates the route and security-group path to the target servers.
Details.errorCorrection: Inbound endpoints accept queries into the VPC, static private records are not a substitute when corporate data changes, and NAT is not a DNS target.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Conditional forwarding preserves existing DNS ownership but creates dependency on hybrid reachability and corporate DNS availability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inbound endpoints serve external-to-VPC queries; VPC-to-external DNS forwarding uses outbound endpoints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Duplicating a dynamic corporate namespace in a private zone can create stale or conflicting answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A NAT gateway is not a DNS server or Resolver forwarding target.

items.prompt: A forwarding rule exists, but workloads in a new VPC still use the default AWS answer. What likely configuration is missing?
constraints: The new VPC uses the same Region as the rule.
The rule target servers are reachable from the VPC.
The query suffix matches the rule.

options.text: Associate the forwarding rule with the new VPC and verify that no more-specific conflicting rule takes precedence.
Associate the rule with the organization root because Resolver rules are inherited by every VPC automatically.
Add an internet gateway route because rule association is only required for public DNS.
Change the EC2 instance role because Resolver rule matching is identity-based.

feedback.Reason: Resolver forwarding rules affect associated VPCs, and a new VPC must be included explicitly or through an approved sharing model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The VPC Resolver evaluates associated rules for matching domain names and forwards the query to the rule's target servers through an outbound endpoint. Association is a separate control from rule creation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team associates the rule with the new VPC, checks rule precedence, and tests from the actual workload subnets.
Details.errorCorrection: Organization hierarchy does not automatically associate every VPC, public routing is not required, and IAM roles do not select DNS rules.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central rule sharing reduces duplication but makes association ownership and precedence important.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Resolver rule association is explicit; organization membership alone is not a VPC association.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private DNS forwarding uses the VPC Resolver and hybrid path, not an internet gateway.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Rule matching uses DNS names and associations, not workload IAM roles.

items.prompt: A private hosted-zone record exists, but EC2 instances cannot resolve it. Which VPC prerequisites should be checked first?
constraints: The hosted zone is associated with the VPC.
The instances use the VPC-provided resolver.
The application does not override DNS with a custom resolver.

options.text: Verify that VPC DNS support and DNS hostnames are enabled and that the instance resolver path reaches the VPC Resolver.
Enable an internet gateway because private hosted-zone answers require public DNS recursion.
Attach the hosted zone to the subnet because Route 53 zones are subnet-scoped.
Add an IAM allow for route53:Resolve because DNS queries are authorized API calls.

feedback.Reason: VPC DNS attributes and the resolver path are prerequisites for resolving private hosted-zone records from workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DNS support lets resources query the Amazon-provided resolver, and DNS hostnames supports VPC hostname behavior. A private hosted zone still needs association and a client path to the resolver.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator checks VPC attributes, DHCP options, resolver reachability, and the exact zone name before changing records.
Details.errorCorrection: Internet gateways are not required for private DNS, zones associate with VPCs rather than subnets, and DNS resolution is not a Route 53 API call requiring an IAM action.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Using the VPC Resolver is simple and managed, while custom DNS requires explicit forwarding and availability design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private hosted-zone resolution should remain inside the VPC DNS path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private hosted zones are associated with VPCs, not individual subnets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A DNS query to the VPC Resolver is not an IAM-authorized Route 53 API request.

items.prompt: An internal service moves between load balancers, but clients should retain the name api.internal.example.com. Which record pattern reduces application changes?
constraints: The target is an AWS load balancer.
Clients resolve through an associated private hosted zone.
The service owner can update DNS records.

options.text: Create a private alias record for the stable service name that targets the internal load balancer and update the alias during controlled migration.
Hard-code the load balancer IP addresses because aliases cannot target AWS load balancers.
Publish the internal name in a public zone so clients can follow every load-balancer change.
Use a NAT gateway as the DNS alias target for the application service.

feedback.Reason: A Route 53 alias can keep a stable private name while targeting an AWS load balancer without hard-coding changing node addresses.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Alias records target supported AWS resources such as load balancers and are resolved by Route 53 in the applicable private zone. The load balancer remains responsible for its own listener and target behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service owner updates the private alias during a staged migration and verifies that clients use the intended internal target.
Details.errorCorrection: Load-balancer IPs can change, public publication violates the internal boundary, and NAT gateways are not DNS record targets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stable aliases reduce client coupling but require DNS ownership and TTL-aware rollout planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Clients should not depend on changing load-balancer node IP addresses when an alias target is available.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An internal service name should remain in the private DNS view when it is not public.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A NAT gateway is a network egress device, not an application DNS target.

items.prompt: A company needs an application entry point reachable only from connected VPCs and on-premises networks. Which load-balancer and DNS combination fits?
constraints: The application is not internet-facing.
The connected networks have private routes to the service VPC.
Clients should use a stable internal name.

options.text: Use an internal load balancer in private subnets and publish its stable name through an associated private hosted zone.
Use an internet-facing load balancer and rely on a private security group to make its public DNS name internal.
Use a NAT gateway as the inbound application endpoint because it accepts connections from every VPC.
Use a gateway endpoint because endpoint routes automatically load-balance application requests.

feedback.Reason: An internal load balancer plus private DNS provides a private ingress boundary for connected clients.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An internal load balancer has private addresses in the VPC. A private hosted-zone record gives clients a stable name, while route and security controls determine which networks can reach it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect associates the zone with approved VPCs, forwards on-premises DNS when needed, and allows only the required client sources and listener ports.
Details.errorCorrection: An internet-facing scheme exposes a public path, NAT gateways are outbound translation devices, and gateway endpoints are for supported AWS services.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Private ingress reduces exposure but requires hybrid routing, DNS association, and health monitoring for the internal path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A public load balancer creates an internet-facing boundary that is not required for private clients.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NAT gateways do not accept inbound application connections.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Gateway endpoints do not load-balance arbitrary application traffic.

items.prompt: The internal DNS name resolves, but clients in a peered VPC time out when connecting to the service. Which layer must be verified before changing DNS?
constraints: The private zone is associated with the client VPC.
The service load balancer is healthy.
The VPCs use non-overlapping CIDRs.

options.text: Verify routes in both VPCs, the peering or transit attachment path, and security controls for the resolved destination before changing the record.
Create a second private hosted zone because every timeout proves the DNS answer is invalid.
Add a NAT gateway route because private ingress traffic must be translated before reaching a load balancer.
Change the client IAM role because private load-balancer reachability is controlled by identity permissions.

feedback.Reason: Successful DNS resolution does not imply that the resolved private address is routable or allowed from the client network.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Private DNS supplies a destination address; VPC routes, return routes, security groups, network ACLs, and the inter-VPC attachment provide the packet path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The responder confirms the resolved address, traces both route tables and the attachment, and checks the listener port and security controls before touching DNS.
Details.errorCorrection: A timeout can occur after correct resolution, NAT is not required for private ingress, and IAM roles do not authorize packets to a load balancer.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separating DNS evidence from route evidence avoids masking a network segmentation defect with record changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The existing record can be correct while the network path is missing or blocked.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private inter-VPC ingress should use the designed private attachment and routes, not NAT egress.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM authorization does not replace VPC routing and packet filtering.

items.prompt: Several spoke VPCs must send internet egress through one inspection VPC, while private AWS service traffic should use endpoints locally. Which principle is essential?
constraints: The organization has a routing hub.
The inspection VPC owns the approved egress path.
AWS service endpoints are deployed in the spoke VPCs where required.

options.text: Use explicit hub-and-spoke routes for general egress and more-specific endpoint routes for private service destinations, documenting which traffic is inspected.
Use one default route for every destination because endpoint routes cannot coexist with centralized egress.
Use DNS records alone to force packets through the inspection VPC without changing route tables.
Use IAM policies to select the egress VPC based on the workload role.

feedback.Reason: Central egress and local private endpoints are separate routing decisions that can coexist through explicit route specificity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route tables choose the most specific matching destination. A local endpoint route can keep supported service traffic private while a default route sends other destinations to the centralized inspection and NAT path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network team validates endpoint routes, hub return routes, and the inspection policy, then tests service and internet destinations separately.
Details.errorCorrection: A single default route can hairpin or bypass intended endpoints, DNS does not steer arbitrary packet paths, and IAM does not choose route tables.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized egress improves governance but increases hub dependency and route-table complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More-specific endpoint routes can coexist with a default route and preserve private service paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS names do not replace the route-table design that forwards packets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Workload identity does not select the VPC egress route.

items.prompt: Private instances need outbound software updates but must not accept unsolicited internet connections. Which path matches the requirement?
constraints: The instances are in private subnets.
The VPC has a public subnet with an internet gateway route.
Inbound internet initiation must remain blocked.

options.text: Route the private subnet's default traffic to a NAT gateway in a public subnet and keep no direct internet-gateway route from the private subnet.
Attach an internet gateway directly to the private subnet because private means the instances have no public IPs.
Use a public hosted zone as the egress security boundary.
Use a security group with an inbound allow from 0.0.0.0/0 because NAT gateways block all return traffic.

feedback.Reason: A NAT gateway provides outbound translation for private subnet resources without making the private subnet directly internet-routable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The private route table sends default traffic to the NAT gateway, and the NAT gateway uses an internet gateway path from its public subnet. Return traffic is statefully associated with outbound flows; unsolicited inbound initiation is not provided.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect places NAT gateways according to the AZ and resilience requirement, restricts security groups, and measures which destinations truly require NAT.
Details.errorCorrection: An internet gateway route from the private subnet is a public path, DNS is not a security boundary, and broad inbound rules weaken the requirement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: NAT improves private egress isolation but adds hourly and data-processing cost and can become an AZ or centralized-egress dependency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private subnet egress uses a route to NAT rather than a direct internet-gateway route.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS records do not enforce packet egress or inbound behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT does not require an internet-wide inbound security-group rule and security groups are stateful.

items.prompt: Security operations needs to identify which VPC workloads queried a suspicious internal hostname. Which evidence source is most direct?
constraints: Queries use the Amazon VPC Resolver.
The organization can centralize logs.
The investigation needs source identity and query time.

options.text: Enable Route 53 Resolver query logging to a protected destination and correlate query records with VPC, source, and time context.
Use an IAM policy simulator because DNS queries are recorded as IAM authorization decisions.
Inspect only the route table because it stores historical DNS queries.
Publish the internal name publicly so public DNS logs identify the private workload.

feedback.Reason: Resolver query logging records DNS query activity from VPC resources and is the appropriate DNS-specific evidence path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route 53 Resolver query logging can deliver query records to supported destinations. The records should be protected and correlated with workload and network telemetry for attribution.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team enables logging before the incident, queries the central destination for the name and time window, and preserves the evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM simulation and route tables do not contain DNS query history, and public publication violates the private namespace boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Query logging improves detection and investigation but creates log volume, retention, and sensitive-name handling considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM simulation evaluates permissions and does not record DNS queries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route tables describe forwarding paths and do not store historical DNS requests.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Making an internal name public weakens privacy and is not an evidence strategy.

items.prompt: A private hosted zone is associated with VPC A, but VPC B connected through a network attachment cannot resolve its records. What should be checked?
constraints: VPC B has a valid route to the service addresses.
The VPCs use the same Region or a supported cross-Region design.
The record should remain private.

options.text: Associate the private hosted zone with VPC B or use a supported centralized DNS association design; network connectivity alone does not share the zone.
Assume peering, Transit Gateway, or RAM automatically makes every private hosted zone visible to connected VPCs.
Add a public DNS record because connected VPCs cannot use private hosted zones.
Add an internet gateway route because private hosted-zone associations are public-network features.

feedback.Reason: Private hosted-zone resolution and network reachability are separate relationships; the client VPC needs an explicit zone association or supported sharing pattern.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A connected VPC can route to an address without being authoritative for the private name. Route 53 association authorization and association determine which VPCs receive private-zone answers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The DNS owner authorizes and associates the client VPC, then tests resolver behavior and network reachability separately.
Details.errorCorrection: Network attachments and RAM do not automatically expose every private zone, public records are unnecessary, and internet routing is outside the private DNS path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized private DNS reduces duplicate zones but requires careful cross-account association ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Network connectivity or resource sharing does not by itself associate a private hosted zone with a VPC.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Publishing a private name publicly weakens the intended resolution boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Private-zone resolution does not require an internet gateway route.

items.prompt: Corporate DNS resolution is a production dependency, but both Resolver endpoint IPs are in one Availability Zone. Which improvement is strongest?
constraints: The VPC spans multiple AZs.
On-premises clients depend on inbound queries.
The organization accepts the endpoint cost for higher availability.

options.text: Place Resolver endpoint IPs in subnets across multiple AZs, allow DNS traffic from approved sources, and test an AZ failure.
Use one endpoint IP because Route 53 Resolver automatically relocates it to every AZ.
Place the endpoint only in a public subnet so all AZs can reach it through the internet.
Add more private hosted-zone records because records provide endpoint availability.

feedback.Reason: Resolver endpoint availability follows the endpoint IP placement, so multiple AZs reduce a single-AZ DNS dependency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Resolver endpoints use ENI addresses in selected subnets. Routing and security groups must allow DNS traffic to those addresses from the intended clients.
Details.scenarioApplication: The DNS owner selects subnets across AZs, publishes the reachable addresses to the forwarding configuration, and performs an AZ failure test.
Details.errorCorrection: Endpoint placement is not automatically replicated to every AZ, public placement is unnecessary, and records do not create endpoint capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multi-AZ endpoint placement costs more but protects a shared DNS dependency from one AZ failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Resolver endpoint IP placement is configured by selected subnets and is not an automatic every-AZ relocation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Hybrid DNS endpoints should use private connectivity and appropriate subnet placement, not public exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Hosted-zone records do not make the Resolver endpoint itself highly available.

items.prompt: An application reports that an internal name does not exist. Which diagnostic order best separates association, resolver, record, and network issues?
constraints: The application runs in a private subnet.
The zone and record were recently changed.
The responder can query from the workload subnet.

options.text: Confirm the query name and client resolver, VPC DNS attributes, private-zone association, record state, Resolver rule precedence, and then reachability to the returned address.
Change the application to a public IP before checking whether the private zone is associated with its VPC.
Add a NAT gateway because NXDOMAIN proves that DNS queries are blocked by private routing.
Replace the private hosted zone with an IAM policy because records are not runtime configuration.

feedback.Reason: A disciplined DNS diagnosis checks the resolver context and authoritative configuration before changing the application or network boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NXDOMAIN or no answer can result from the wrong resolver, missing zone association, stale record, or forwarding precedence. If an address is returned, packet routing and security controls become the next layer.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator reproduces the query from the workload subnet, checks zone association and rules, then tests the returned address without broadening exposure.
Details.errorCorrection: Public exposure is an unsafe first response, NAT does not repair a missing DNS record, and IAM policies are not Route 53 record data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layered diagnosis takes longer than a bypass but preserves private naming and produces evidence for the real fault.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A private DNS failure should be diagnosed before exposing or changing the application path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NXDOMAIN is an answer or resolver-context problem, not proof that NAT is missing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM policies do not replace Route 53 record configuration or DNS associations.

items.prompt: A security team requires all general internet egress from a spoke VPC to cross a centralized inspection VPC. Which review finding is a bypass?
constraints: The spoke has a transit gateway attachment.
The inspection VPC provides the approved NAT path.
Private endpoint routes are intentionally local exceptions.

options.text: A spoke route table with a direct NAT or internet-gateway path for general destinations bypasses the required centralized inspection route.
A more-specific gateway endpoint route for S3 is necessarily a bypass even when the policy explicitly permits local private service access.
A private hosted-zone association is a packet bypass because DNS records always override route tables.
A Resolver query log is a bypass because logs route DNS queries to the public internet.

feedback.Reason: The direct general-egress path defeats the centralized inspection boundary; intentionally local private-service routes are a different, documented policy decision.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Route tables select paths by destination specificity. A direct default route to NAT or an internet gateway can avoid the hub, while a permitted service endpoint route can keep supported service traffic private by design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network reviewer inventories every default and specific route, compares them with the egress policy, and removes only unauthorized general-egress paths.
Details.errorCorrection: An approved endpoint exception is not automatically a bypass, DNS associations do not forward packets, and query logging records activity rather than routing it publicly.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized egress gives consistent inspection but must document and monitor intentional local endpoint exceptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A documented endpoint route can be an intentional private-service exception rather than unauthorized general egress.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Hosted-zone association affects name resolution and does not override packet route selection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Resolver query logging is an evidence destination and does not make application egress public.
